abstract_sentences.text: While language models achieve impressive results, their learning dynamics are far from understood.

evidence.anchor: learning dynamics are far from understood

abstract_sentences.text: Many domains of interest – such as natural language syntax, coding languages, arithmetic – are captured by context-free grammars (CFGs).
In this work, we extend prior work on neural language modeling of CFGs in a novel direction: how language modeling behaves with respect to CFG substructure, namely subgrammars.
We define subgrammars, and prove a set of fundamental theorems connecting language modeling and subgrammars.

evidence.anchor: prove a set of fundamental theorems

abstract_sentences.text: We show that language modeling loss recurses linearly over its top-level subgrammars; applied recursively, the loss decomposes into losses for “irreducible” subgrammars.
Under additional assumptions, and empirically, parametrized models learn subgrammars in parallel, unlike children who first master simple substructures.

We find that subgrammar pretraining can improve final performance, but only for tiny models relative to the grammar, while alignment analyses show that pretraining consistently leads to internal representations that better reflect the grammar’s substructure.

evidence.anchor: only for tiny models relative to the grammar

claim_closure.claim: CFGs have a usable inner/outer subgrammar structure.
claim_closure.method_response: Definitions 3.3/3.5 formalize inner/outer structures; Theorem 4.1 defines the unique hierarchy.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Appendix D instantiates the structures in seven PCFG families.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: §7 returns to CFG substructure; Appendix C supplies proofs.

claim_closure.claim: LM loss recurses linearly over top-level and then irreducible subgrammars.
claim_closure.method_response: Proposition 3.9 connects MLE and KL; Theorem 4.3, Corollaries 4.4/4.5/C.1, and Theorem 4.6 state the recurrence under their conditions.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figures 1, 2, and 5 visualize decomposed KL trajectories.

claim_closure.claim: Small Transformers learn subgrammars in parallel.
claim_closure.method_response: Corollary 4.7 gives a sufficient independence condition for gradient descent.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figures 1–2 show parallel-looking declines in the selected synthetic examples.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: §7 says models tend to reduce error in parallel; §8 says there is no full theory for when/why.

evidence.anchor: do not have a full theory

claim_closure.claim: Subgrammar pretraining can improve final performance only for tiny models relative to the grammar.
claim_closure.method_response: §5.2 matches total epochs and sentences and varies pretraining exposure.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 6 and Appendix E.3 compare 30-seed distributions; two- and four-layer panels differ visually.

claim_closure.claim: Pretraining yields representations more aligned with grammar substructure.
claim_closure.method_response: §5.2 and Appendix B define CKA/cosine measurements across seeds and sequence types.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Tables 1, 3, and 4 report selected alignment improvements and mixed layer/type effects.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: §7 says representations are more aligned but leaves why and benefits open.

claim_closure.claim: Low-loss LMs do not robustly generalize syntax at deeper recursion.
claim_closure.method_response: Nested Parentheses distinguishes length extension from recursive depth under identical target distributions.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figures 4 and 7 show higher deep-recursion prediction error; the 5/5 versus 2/5 frontier anecdote is small.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: §8 leaves representational versus optimization causes unresolved.

evidence.anchor: struggle with depth and not length

claim_closure.claim: Completed prefix context and grammatical validity have little effect relative to recursive depth.
claim_closure.method_response: Three prefix conditions are set up in Appendix E.4.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Figure 7 endpoint labels are approximately .166, .166, .163; no uncertainty is shown.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: No broader claim is added in §7.

lexical_rhetoric.scope: Manual context coding only; raw token counts are delegated to the aggregate script. References, equations, table values, and template boilerplate are excluded.

claim_verbs.we demonstrate: not observed as a repeated core-claim formula

lexical_rhetoric.interpretation: Strong language clusters around formally conditioned theorems; empirical passages use more qualifiers. Repetition is driven by domain objects and inference actions rather than generic impact language.

final_judgment.single_storyline: The paper turns CFG inner/outer subgrammars into recursive LM-loss units, then uses that structure to study parallel learning, pretraining-induced representations, and recursion depth failure. [p.1 Abstract; p.3–6 §§3–4]
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: Definitions, core theorem statements, Figures 1–4, Table 1, directional interpretation, and an explicit §8 remain in the main body. [p.3–9]
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Proofs, architecture/hyperparameters, all PCFG productions, supplemental CKA/cosine/final-KL/prefix results move to Appendices A–E. The main storyline is intelligible, but exact reproduction and strength checks require the appendix. [p.12–21]
final_judgment.best_pattern: Definition 4.2 gives conditioned-KL meaning; Theorems 4.3/4.5 and Figure 1 then align the algebraic terms with identically labeled curves. [p.4–5]
final_judgment.largest_gap: Parallel-learning evidence does not measure the Corollary 4.7 independence condition, and the pretraining-benefit magnitude is constrained by model scope plus Table/Figure reporting tensions. Deep-failure cause remains unresolved. [p.6; p.9; p.21]
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For a recursively decomposable object, put definition, compositional theorem, and item-labelled observable curves in one continuous argument so readers can map the identity to measurements. [p.4–6]
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This rule requires a defined generative decomposition and measurable terms; the paper does not establish transfer to ambiguous CFGs, natural language, grammar induction, other Chomsky classes, or large-model training without verified independence. [p.9]
